title: Convexifications of rank-one-based substructures in QCQPs and applications to the pooling problem
contribution: Characterizes when the convex hull of a nonnegative rank-1 matrix set with linear side constraints is polyhedral or SOC-representable, with polynomial-time linear optimization. Recasts generalized pooling as rank-1 constraints on flow-decomposition matrices and derives new LP/MILP relaxations and restrictions that improve dual bounds on three instance sets (read in arXiv v1).
problem_entry: After the rank-1 lift, all QCQP nonconvexity sits in rank(W)<=1; beyond the boolean quadric polytope, no structured side constraints had been studied, and pooling naturally produces row/column-bounded rank-1 sets (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Convexify {W>=0 : <A^k,W> <= b_k, rank W <= 1}: polyhedral for A^k = alpha^k beta^T, SOCr for two constraints or for structured rank-2 A^k. Rewrite pooling bilinear terms as rank-1 matrices, and read the hull's extended formulation as McCormick on a ratio variable, which can be discretized into MILP relaxations and restrictions (pp. 3-13).
assumptions: QCQP over [0,1]^n; nonnegative rank-1 matrices; boundedness. Thm 1 needs A^k = alpha^k beta^T with beta>0 and condition (8). Thm 3 needs n1=n2>=3 and A^k = alpha^k beta beta^T + gamma^k delta delta^T with nonnegative coefficients. Pooling: linear objective, pool-to-pool arcs allowed (pp. 1-11).
proof_devices: Extreme-point support bound by a rank-1 perturbation W+- = x(y +- eps...)^T that keeps active constraints tight (pp. 4-7)
Hull written as the convex hull of a union of small-support pieces, each one quadratic over a polytope, SOCr by cited result [47] (p. 6)
Disjunctive extended formulation with weights t_j, shown exact because its extreme points have exactly one positive t (pp. 4-5)
Fourier-Motzkin projection to partition inequalities with O(n1 n2) separation (App. A.1-A.2, pp. 23-28)
Non-polyhedrality shown by a curve of extreme points and the strict convexity of u^2/(1-u) (Prop. 12, pp. 28-29)
Binary-expansion discretization of the ratio variable, giving an outer (Prop. 4) and an inner (Prop. 5) approximation (pp. 10-11)
experiments: Gurobi 7.5.1 on a stated PC. Instances: 24 real Mining, 12 Literature (28 of 40 dropped because pq closes their gap), and 24 new Random generalized-pooling instances, posted online. MILP restrictions give primal bounds (H=3, 1800 s). Nine LP relaxations in Light/Medium/Heavy tiers and six MILP relaxations, measured by percentage duality gap and time. F^S_2 cap F^T_2 beats the heavy F^ST_1; no single MILP relaxation wins everywhere (pp. 17-23).
positioning: Prefers set convexification to function envelopes. Builds on the BQP hull and on the SOCr result for one quadratic over a polytope, and contrasts with two-quadratic SOCr results, whose technique differs. A known-vs-new table shows the pq/tp/stp pooling relaxations as special cases (pp. 2, 6, 16).
writing: Previews each section's contribution; flags the key move ('Our key observation'); gives dead ends in one line with reasons; states the open case as a conjecture; hedges the concluding superlative with 'on average' (pp. 2-3, 9, 12-16, 23).
limits_future: No hull description for row-and-column bounds beyond 2x2 (optimizing over it conjectured NP-hard); joint row-column discretization too large; F^ST_2 numerically unstable; no single best MILP relaxation; the new Random set is offered as a benchmark (pp. 9, 13, 16, 20, 23).

method_links.note: States the substructure paradigm; the rank-1 lift carries all nonconvexity; pooling chooses the side constraints; convexifies the set with constructive extended formulations.
Cheap LP ('Light') relaxations and MILP discretizations certify duality gaps on stated hardware; Light LP is nearly as strong as the heavier relaxations.
Boundary shown: the row-and-column hull is SOCr but not polyhedral, with an explicit extreme-point family; the general case is left as a conjecture.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: paired MILP relaxation and restriction from one discretized ratio variable
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The hull's extended formulation equals McCormick on the ratio t_j. Discretizing t_j gives an outer set (relaxation) and an inner set (restriction), used for dual and primal bounds.

transferable: Rewrite bilinear equalities that share one multiplier as a rank-1 constraint on a matrix of disaggregated (source- or terminal-indexed) flow variables, then convexify it row-wise and column-wise (pp. 12-16).
Bound the support of extreme points of a rank-1 set with m linear constraints by a homogeneous-system perturbation, then convexify each small support pattern and take the union (pp. 4-7).
Prove non-polyhedrality by exhibiting a one-parameter family of extreme points through a strictly convex function (p. 29).
Drop benchmark instances that the baseline relaxation already closes, say so, and report a table of the best average per tier (pp. 17, 23).
When the heaviest relaxation runs out of memory, put the best bound from the other methods in parentheses and say so, so that the averages stay comparable (pp. 18-19).

quotes.text: Observe that all the non-convexity of the problem is now captured by the rank-1 condition.
It is well-known that it is possible to obtain tighter convex relaxations when convexifing a set directly rather than using convex envelopes of functions describing the set.

title: Branch-and-bound solves random binary ips in polytime
contribution: Proves that standard best-bound branch-and-bound with variable branching, branching on any fractional variable, explores only polynomially many nodes with good probability on random binary packing IPs with a fixed number of constraints. Also gives a deterministic tree bound for 'well-behaved' IPs (read in the arXiv v4 revision, which the text calls a significant improvement over the SODA version).
problem_entry: Variable branching powers all MILP solvers and trees are small in practice, yet no theory explains this and worst cases are exponential. To avoid worst-case lower bounds, the paper analyses random instances, as smoothed analysis did for the simplex method (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Tree size <= 2|G|n+1, where G is the set of 0/1 points whose reduced-cost loss is at most the integrality gap. Good points can only flip items whose columns lie near the LP's separating hyperplane, and random columns rarely lie near any hyperplane (uniform slab bound), which gives n^{O(m)} (pp. 6-14).
assumptions: max c^T x s.t. Ax<=b, x binary; A and c i.i.d. uniform on [0,1]; b_j = beta_j n with beta_j in (0,1/2); m fixed, n>=m+1; best-bound node selection; only pruning by bound used; Dyer-Frieze integrality gap O(log^2 n / n) (pp. 2-5).
proof_devices: Best-bound never branches on a node whose LP value is below IP* (Lemma 1, pp. 4-5)
At most m fractional coordinates at an LP vertex (Lemma 2, p. 5)
Lagrangian saddle point bounds the reduced-cost loss at branched nodes by the integrality gap (Lemma 3, p. 7)
Internal nodes charged to good points, at most n-to-1 by a lowest-common-ancestor argument (Lemmas 4-5, Thm 3, pp. 7-8)
Flip cost >= distance of the column to the hyperplane H; dyadic distance buckets and a counting product (Lemmas 6-7, pp. 8-10)
Uniform slab bound over all hyperplanes from an eps-net, discretized widths, Ball's cube slicing, Bernstein's inequality and a union bound (Thm 4, pp. 11-13)
positioning: Contrasts with Lenstra and Pataki et al. ('very heavy machinery') and with custom enumeration schemes for random knapsacks, which are not general B&B. Builds on Dyer-Frieze. Notes follow-ups by Borst et al. (Gaussian data) and Frieze (exponential lower bound for ATSP) (pp. 2-3, 5).
writing: Main theorem in the introduction, followed by three remarks on practical relevance (best-bound optimality, any variable choice, only bound-pruning used). The 'first known' claim is hedged as 'an indication'. Changes from the SODA version are stated (pp. 1-4).
limits_future: Fixed m, with the exponent growing in m; uniform packing model; best-bound selection; no matching lower bound. The deterministic Corollary 3 needs a small gap and no concentration of columns near hyperplanes. No explicit future-work list (pp. 3, 11, 15).

method_links.note: An unexplained solver habit (variable branching) is cut down to a provable proxy (random instances, best-bound) because the worst case is exponential; the paper returns to practice through its 'indication' remarks.
The boundary is drawn through sufficient conditions (fixed m; small gap, no column concentration), not through a tight example or a lower bound.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: count near-optimal solutions to bound enumeration effort
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Tree size is bounded by the number of 0/1 points whose reduced-cost loss is within the integrality gap, and those points are then counted geometrically.

transferable: Bound a B&B tree by counting near-optimal integer points and charging nodes to them with bounded multiplicity (pp. 6-8).
When the object to control depends on the random data, prove a uniform bound over all such objects with an eps-net and a union bound instead of conditioning (pp. 11-13).
Analyse the rule with an arbitrary, even adversarial, choice inside it, so that any practical refinement inherits the bound (p. 3).
Use the LP's Lagrangian saddle point to write a 0/1 point's suboptimality as per-item reduced costs, each bounded below by a distance to a hyperplane (pp. 6, 8-9).
Keep the deterministic links of a lemma chain separate from the probabilistic ones, so that they give a corollary for general instances (p. 15).

quotes.text: In order to avoid worst-case lower bounds, a standard idea is to consider random instances.
We believe that this result provides an indication as to why branch-and-bound with variable branching works so well in practice.

title: Complexity of training ReLU neural network
contribution: Shows that exact training of the fully connected two-hidden-layer (2,1)-ReLU network is NP-hard. Training k-ReLU networks is polynomial when the input dimension and width are fixed, and polynomial (randomized) when there are N first-layer nodes for N data points.
problem_entry: The complexity of training fully connected multi-layer ReLU networks was open, and earlier ReLU hardness results used an artificially restricted (diagonal) architecture. The paper takes Blum-Rivest's 3-node graph and puts ReLU at every node (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: Reduce 2-hyperplane separability to training, using 18 gadget points in two extra dimensions and a 'hard-sorting' characterization of exact fit. Complement this with hyperplane-arrangement enumeration plus convex QPs for fixed (d,k), and with a reduction to one-hidden-layer interpolation for N nodes (pp. 4-15).
assumptions: Exact-fit decision version with labels {0,1}; weights normalized to +-1 by positive homogeneity; 0 in S1 after translation. Thm 3.3 uses square loss with d and k constant; Prop. 3.4 assumes distinct inputs and y>=0 (pp. 5, 8, 13-15).
proof_devices: Polynomial reduction from 2-hyperplane separability with 18 fixed gadget points in two added coordinates (pp. 7-9)
Hard-sorting characterization: exact fit holds iff the first-layer output is constant on label-1 points and strictly lower on label-0 points (Lemma 4.5, p. 10; A.4, pp. 16-17)
Subset monotonicity of hard-sorting, used in contrapositive form (Remark 4.3, pp. 10-11)
The gadget forces w1=w2=-1 and c=0, via pigeonhole, non-collinearity, a case analysis on parallel normals and T1 subset conv(T0) (Lemma 4.7; A.5-A.7, pp. 11, 17-19)
Hyperplane-arrangement enumeration with O(N^d) partitions per node, plus one convex QP per pattern and sign case (A.1, pp. 13-15)
Labels padded with zeros for (2,j) outputs (A.8, p. 20)
positioning: Extends the Blum-Rivest/Megiddo threshold hardness to ReLU. Criticizes Livni et al. and DasGupta et al. for artificial architecture restrictions. Separates worst-case NP-hardness from distributional and SQ hardness. Generalizes Arora et al.'s fixed-dimension algorithm and notes concurrent single-node ReLU hardness (pp. 2-6).
writing: Bulleted contributions with theorem numbers; prose proof sketches before the formal results; a lemma chain in the body with proofs in the appendix; a geometric figure for hard-sorting; an 'in our opinion' claim of resolving a significant gap (pp. 4, 6, 10, 13).
limits_future: Open: the complexity for 2 < k < N, and generalizing the gadget to k-ReLU. Only the exact-fit decision version is treated; the Thm 3.3 exponent grows as (2^k-1)d; Prop. 3.4 is randomized (pp. 5, 7, 13, 15).

method_links.note: Positive and negative results are paired: NP-hard at k=2, polynomial for fixed d and k and at k=N. The middle range is named as open, and dropping fixed d flips the complexity.
Motivated by the empirical success of over-parameterized networks and gives a matching polynomial case, but does not claim to explain gradient training.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: gadget plus characterization lemma for hardness of a continuous model
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: An exact geometric characterization (hard-sorting) sits between the training problem and the NP-complete source problem, and a fixed gadget pins down the signs and weights of any solution.

transferable: When earlier proofs rely on an artificial restriction, re-ask the hardness question on the exact unrestricted model that practitioners use (p. 3).
Put an exact characterization lemma between the target problem and the NP-complete source, so that the reduction argues about geometry, not weights (pp. 9-10).
Use a small fixed gadget in added coordinates to force the sign pattern of any feasible solution, then reason only about the original coordinates (pp. 8-12).
Normalize weights by positive homogeneity (w[ax+b]+ = sgn(w)[|w|(ax+b)]+) before the case analysis (p. 5).
For polynomiality in fixed dimension, enumerate activation patterns using the hyperplane-arrangement bound and solve one convex program per pattern (pp. 6, 13-15).

quotes.text: The architecture artificially restricts the form of the affine functions in order to prove NP-hardness.
Techniques used in the proof are different from earlier work in the literature because there is no combinatorial interpretation to ReLU as opposed to the threshold function.
